question: Spread 3 claps as evenly as you can over 8 pulses. Why does the result sound like a groove you already know?
answer: Because it is one: 3+3+2, the tresillo, under the habanera and countless pop grooves. Godfried Toussaint showed in 2005 that this rule, used by Eric Bjorklund to space pulses at a neutron source, generates dozens of traditional rhythms. Five over eight gives the Cuban cinquillo.
move: When a pattern feels natural, look for the simple rule that makes it.
ask: Which pattern in my life feels natural but comes from one simple rule?

scene.hint: The kick marks the beat. Add one pattern at a time over it.

tracks.text: The tresillo: three notes spread as evenly as 8 pulses allow, 3, 3, then 2.

tracks.name: Five
tracks.pattern: X . x x . x x . X . x x . x x .
tracks.text: Five spread as evenly as 8 allow: the Cuban cinquillo. Same rule.

tracks.name: Clave
tracks.text: Son clave: the same 3, 3, 2 to open, then two hits to answer it.

moments.name: Locked
moments.text: Bass and clave open together, then the clave answers alone. That is the groove.

reference: Toussaint, The Euclidean algorithm generates traditional musical rhythms, Proceedings of BRIDGES: Mathematical Connections in Art, Music and Science, 2005
